title: Best Dehumidifier for Drywall (2026): Mud, Plaster & New Builds
h1: The Best Dehumidifiers for Drying Drywall and Plaster
dek: Joint compound, plaster and wet wallboard all dry on the air's schedule. A construction dehumidifier puts you back in charge of it.
description: The best dehumidifier for drywall, mud and plaster drying: LGR construction units, a compact one-room pick and a budget setup, plus target moisture readings.
intro: A **dehumidifier for drywall** earns its keep in two situations: a renovation or new build where joint compound and plaster won't dry fast enough to keep the schedule, and a leak or flood where wet wallboard has to dry before mold gets a foothold. In both cases, the three things that matter most are drying power at moderate humidity, hands-off drainage so the unit can run overnight, and how many amps it pulls from the circuit you have. Our top pick, the **AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme**, gets all three right for a typical floor of a house.

For a single room, the compact **Dri-Eaz Revolution** is easier to carry up the stairs, and for an entire new build the **Dri-Eaz LGR 7000XLi** is the contractor-grade answer. If you're just finishing one patch or a small bathroom, a regular household 50-pint unit and a good fan will do the job for a fraction of the cost.
topPicksLead: The **AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme** is our top pick for drying drywall because it keeps pulling water as the air gets drier, pumps it away on its own and runs on an ordinary household circuit.

sections.heading: How we pick dehumidifiers for drying drywall

blocks.text: We compared units on the specs that decide a drying job: capacity under AHAM and saturation conditions for restoration units, the 2019 DOE rating for household models, amp draw, pump lift, weight and listed noise. We also read manuals, restoration drying guidance and owner reviews from contractors and DIY renovators.
We don't lab-test units ourselves. Every rating here is the manufacturer's figure, with its test conditions noted.

sections.heading: How to choose a construction dehumidifier

items.label: Match the machine to the project
items.text: One room or a small leak suits a compact LGR or a household 50-pint unit. A full floor calls for a Storm-class LGR. A whole new build or gut renovation may need a 7000XLi-class unit or several machines.
sub: Closed doors shrink the space you have to dry
Our [dehumidifier size guide](/guides/dehumidifier-size-guide/) covers everyday pint math

items.label: Choose LGR for wet walls
items.text: Low-grain refrigerant units keep removing water as the air drops into the 40s and as rooms cool. Household units slow down sharply there, which is exactly when wet drywall still needs help.

items.label: Insist on a pump
items.text: A drying job runs day and night. A built-in pump that sends water to a sink, window or drain means no full bucket stalls the job at 2 a.m.

items.label: Count the amps
items.text: A household 15-amp circuit should carry no more than about 12 amps continuously. Add up the dehumidifier, fans and any space heater before you plug in, and spread big units across circuits.

items.label: Keep it warm, not hot
items.text: Compound makers generally want the room at 55°F or warmer while finishing. Heat speeds drying, but blasting a fresh coat with a heater can cause cracking and shrinkage.

items.label: Measure, don't guess
items.text: Use a hygrometer for the room and a pin or pinless moisture meter for the wall. A [reliable hygrometer](/best/best-hygrometer/) tells you when the air is ready; the meter tells you when the board is.

items.label: Weigh rental vs. buying
items.text: For a single project, renting an LGR from a tool or equipment rental counter can make more sense. If you'll reuse it in a crawl space or basement, buying wins quickly.

sections.heading: When is drywall dry enough? Target readings

blocks.text: There's no single magic number, so professionals compare. Take a reading from an unaffected wall in the same house — the *dry standard* — and keep drying until the wet area reads the same. Most moisture meters have a gypsum or drywall scale; use it rather than the wood setting.

blocks.title: When to cut, not dry
blocks.text: Drywall that sags, crumbles, smells musty or shows visible mold should be replaced, along with any wet insulation behind it. Water from sewage or floodwater calls for replacement too. Our [water damage dehumidifier guide](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-water-damage/) and [mold guide](/guides/does-a-dehumidifier-help-with-mold/) cover the bigger picture.

sections.heading: Drying plaster, mud and new builds

blocks.text: Drying-type compound loses water to the air, so humidity directly sets its pace. Setting-type compound (hot mud) hardens chemically in its stated time, but still has to dry before you prime. Run the dehumidifier with the room closed and a fan raking across the walls, and you can often get to the next coat the following morning.

Gypsum veneer plaster sets quickly and can be dried with a dehumidifier once it has set; follow the maker's guidance before painting. Traditional lime plaster is different: it cures slowly by taking in carbon dioxide and can crack if forced dry. For lime, run a dehumidifier gently to keep the room from getting clammy, not to bake the walls.

A new house dries out for months as concrete, lumber, mud and primer give up water. A construction dehumidifier during finishing helps prevent nail pops, slow-drying seams and paint problems, and protects freshly installed trim and [hardwood floors](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-wood-floors/) from absorbing that moisture. Once you're painting, our [paint drying picks](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-paint-drying/) take over.

blocks.text: Drywall and plaster dry on the air's schedule unless you change the air. For most renovations, the **AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme** plus a fan cuts days off the job and runs safely on a household circuit. Go compact with the **Dri-Eaz Revolution** for one room, big with the **Dri-Eaz LGR 7000XLi** for a new build, and budget with the **hOmeLabs 50-Pint** for small patches — and confirm the wall is dry with a meter, not a fingertip, before you paint.

faqs.q: Does a dehumidifier help drywall mud dry faster?
faqs.a: Yes. Drying-type joint compound releases water into the air, so lowering humidity speeds it up. A closed room with a dehumidifier and a fan blowing across the walls can often shorten drying to overnight per coat.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier do I need for drying drywall?
faqs.a: For a patch or one small room, a household 50-pint unit is enough. For a full floor, choose an LGR rated around 80–90 pints AHAM, and for a whole new house, a 130-pint-class LGR or several units.

faqs.q: Is a construction dehumidifier rental worth it?
faqs.a: For a single project, often yes. Renting an LGR for a week can cost much less than buying one. If you'll reuse it for a crawl space, basement or future renovations, buying pays off.

faqs.q: How long does wet drywall take to dry with a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: With an LGR and air movement, lightly wet drywall typically dries in about three to five days. Keep drying until your meter reading matches an unaffected wall, and replace board that sags, crumbles or shows mold.

faqs.q: Can I use a dehumidifier for drying plaster?
faqs.a: Yes for gypsum plaster once it has set. Go gently with traditional lime plaster, which cures slowly and can crack if forced dry; use the dehumidifier only to stop the room from getting damp.

faqs.q: What humidity should a room be when finishing drywall?
faqs.a: Aim for roughly 40–50% relative humidity with the room at 55°F or warmer. Much more humid and compound dries slowly; heavy heat on fresh mud can cause shrinkage and cracking.
